L194: # Clinical Trials
L195: 
L196: 【70†Image: dog at vet】
L197: 
L198: Through clinical trials, we can offer our canine companions the best possible care, while also contributing to the advancement of veterinary science for the benefit of all dogs and their human counterparts.
L199: ##### Find More Clinical Trials
L200: 
L201:   * Explore more of 【71†Penn Vet’s clinical trials】 to get involved and learn more about our cutting-edge 【72†cancer research】 at the school.
L202:   * The 【73†AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry†veterinaryclinicaltrials.org】 can also be a resource to help you find a trial for your pet.
L203: ### Clincial Trial for Dogs with Newly Diagnosed Osteosarcoma
L204: 
L205: Contact:
L206: Mary Beth Boland, CVT
L207: mboland@vet.upenn.edu
L208: (215) 898-5098
L209: 
L210: This clinical trial is investigating the ability of genetically engineered CAR-iNKT cells from healthy donor dogs to treat osteosarcoma and delay metastatic disease in newly diagnosed dogs.
L211: 
L212: This clinical trial is fully funded and includes
L213:   * Bone biopsy to diagnose osteosarcoma
L214:   * CAR-iNKT cellular therapy
L215:   * Amputation of affected limb
L216:   * Standard of care chemotherapy after amputation
L217:   * Regular follow up including labwork and chest radiographs
L218: 
L219: 【74†Download Clinical Trial Flyer】
L220: ### Cell Therapy for Metastatic Osteosarcoma
L221: 
L222: View the trial on the 【75†Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry†veterinaryclinicaltrials.org】
L223: 
L224: Contact:
L225: Nicola Mason, BVetMed, PhD, DACVIM, FRCVS
L226: nmason@vet.upenn.edu
L227: (215) 898-3996
L228: In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of a type of white blood cell known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells that are made from the blood of a healthy donor dog. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. In this study, we will use iNKT cells that express a cancer targeting receptor known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the modified iNKT cells to the cancer cells which are then killed.
L229: The CAR-iNKT cells also will further activate the patient’s own immune system to help kill the cancer cells. The purpose of this study is to determine the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, their maximum tolerated dose, how long they will remain in the patient and their effectiveness against bone cancer that has spread to the lungs.
L230: 【76†Download Clinical Trial Flyer】
L231: ### Cellular immunotherapy for the Treatment of B cell Lymphoma or Leukemia
L232: 
L233: View the trial on the 【77†Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry†veterinaryclinicaltrials.org】
L234: 
L235: Contact:
L236: Nicola Mason, BVetMed, PhD, DACVIM, FRCVS
L237: nmason@vet.upenn.edu
L238: (215) 898-3996
L239: 
L240: Mary Beth Boland, CVT
L241: mboland@vet.upenn.edu
L242: (215) 898-5098
L243: The purpose of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of genetically engineered CAR-T cells as a treatment for your dog’s cancer. The CAR-T cells are made from your dog’s own immune cells. Patients will be screened at the University of Pennsylvania’s veterinary hospital to determine their eligibility for the study.
L244: This study will involve a screening visit for medical history and blood tests, a pre-conditioning visit, the treatment visit where the drug is administered, and monthly follow-up visits to assess the safety and effectiveness of the drug to treat your dog’s cancer
L245: 【78†Download Clinical Trial Flyer】
L246: ### Bladder Cancer Study
L247: 
L248: Contact:
L249: Samuel Stewart
L250: sstewart@ethosvet.com
L251: ##### Pilot study to evaluate the safety and pharmacodynamic effects of a fully canine anti-PD1 antibody in pet dogs with urothelial carcinoma
L252: Dogs with urothelial carcinoma may be eligible to participate in a clinical trial. This study seeks to evaluate a novel immunotherapy that specifically targets an important molecule primarily expressed on immune cells. This molecule usually turns off the immune cells and prevents overactive immune responses. However, it also turns off anti-cancer immune responses and prevents the immune system controlling and killing cancer cells.
L253: Immunotherapies that can inhibit this molecule on immune cells that recognize cancer cells could make it possible for the immune system to recognize and attack the underlying cancer more effectively. This study seeks to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of this novel immunotherapy in dogs with urothelial carcinoma.
L254: ### Details of Study
L255: Project Description   | Urothelial carcinoma (also known as transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common type of bladder cancer to affect dogs. Treatment often involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy, with the aim being to reduce the size of the tumor, alleviate symptoms, and improve the dog’s quality of life. In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a promising treatment approach for many types of cancer, including canine urothelial carcinoma.
L256: Immunotherapies aim to harness the body’s immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. They can be particularly attractive for treating cancers that are difficult to access surgically or that have metastasized (spread to other parts of the body).
L257: This study seeks to evaluate a novel immunotherapy when used in dogs with urothelial carcinoma. The therapy specifically targets an important molecule primarily expressed on immune cells, which usually turns off the immune cells and prevents overactive immune responses. However, it also turns off anti-cancer immune responses and prevents the immune system controlling and killing cancer cells.
L258: Immunotherapies that can inhibit this molecule on immune cells that recognize cancer cells could make it possible for the immune system to recognize and attack the underlying cancer more effectively. Urothelial carcinoma in dogs shares many biological and molecular features with human urothelial carcinoma, including their ability to be shielded from the immune system.
L259: Human clinical trials in urothelial carcinoma investigating similar immunotherapies have shown these therapies to be more effective than traditional chemotherapies in some cases. Development of an immunotherapy that is safe and beneficial in canine urothelial carcinoma patients will advance veterinarians ability to treat this disease and will provide an important model to inform future canine and human clinical trials in this area.
L260: This study seeks to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of this novel immunotherapy in dogs with urothelial carcinoma.
L261: Locations  | Veterinary Specialty Hospital – North County San Marcos, California
L262: Colorado Animal Specialty & Emergency, Boulder, Colorado
L263: Study Type   | Interventional
L264: Intervention   | Drug
L265: Inclusion Criteria  |
L266:   * Weigh ≥5kg and ≤35kg
L267:   * Histologically confirmed urothelial carcinoma, with or without documented lymph node involvement (both newly diagnosed dogs and those with recurrent/relapsed disease are eligible)
L268:   * Measurable tumor burden with primary intravesicular tumor amenable for cystoscopic biopsy
L269:   * ECOG performance status of grade 0 or 1
L270:   * Adequate hematologic, hepatic, and renal function
L271:   * Creatinine ≤2.0 mg/dL
L272:   * No significant comorbidities
L273:   * Expected survival time of at least eight weeks
L274:   * Signed informed owner consent
L275: Exclusion Criteria   |
L276:   * Body weight of <5kg or >35kg
L277:   * Pulmonary metastatic disease
L278:   * History of any diagnosed or suspected autoimmune or immune-mediated disease, colitis, IBD, endocrine disorders
L279:   * Significant comorbidities
L280:   * Symptomatic urinary tract infection confirmed on urine culture
L281:   * Any >grade 2 hematologic or biochemical abnormality
L282:   * History of daily drug administration for unregulated chronic disease
L283:   * Prior experimental therapy
L284:   * Prior antibody therapies
L285:   * Prior immunomodulatory therapies within six weeks of study enrollment.
L286:   * Dogs receiving standard of care NSAID for UC for at least two weeks prior to study enrollment will be allowed to continue while on study
L287:   * Concurrent chemotherapy or radiation therapy within two weeks of study enrollment
L288:   * Treatment with corticosteroids within seven days of study enrollment
L289: Potential Medical Benefits to Enrolled Animals   | Possible improvement in the status of your dog’s urothelial carcinoma.
L290: Potential Medical Risks to Enrolled Animals   | The risk for complications from the routine diagnostics and imaging performed for the study are considered to be very low. Several study visits will require sedation or general anesthesia, which can be associated with complications. The veterinarian overseeing your dog’s care will discuss the potential complications associated with the sedation / anesthesia plan they intend to use in your dog.
L291: Financial Incentives for Study Participants   | Fully funded including initial screening

L99: # Clinical trials
L100: 
L101: The School of Veterinary Science has several clinical trials and research studies seeking volunteers and input from the public.
L102: 
L103: Each trial or research study has varying requirements in regards to the assistance the investigators are requiring. We invite you to take a look at the current trials listed below to see if you can contribute.
L104: Please note that all clinical trials and research have animal ethics and/or human ethics approvals, participation is voluntary and any participants can be removed from a trial at any time.
L105: ## Dog bone cancer vaccine trial
L106: We are looking for pet dogs diagnosed with cancer to test an experimental vaccine. The clinical research trial is for dogs recently diagnosed with canine appendicular osteosarcoma, a common bone tumour that affects 10,000 dogs a year globally. In this trial, our researchers will assess two vaccine formulations. To be eligible, dogs need to have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma of long bones of the limbs with no evidence of metastasis, or cancer spread, based on a physical exam and radiographs.
L107: Dogs can be any breed but must be proceeding to surgery to treat their cancer. Read more 【42†about these trials†www.uq.edu.au】.
L108: Applications for the trial can be made via 【43†this webform†survey.app.uq.edu.au】, or questions can be directed to Dr José Granados Soler (j.granados@uq.edu.au).
L109: ## Cattle with lantana camara toxicity
L110: We are looking for cattle that are naturally intoxicated with lantana camara.  Lantana is a common toxic plant in Queensland. We are searching for prognostic indicators of intoxicated cattle to better identify cattle that will survive.
L111: If you have cattle that are showing signs of photosensitization and have access to lantana, we would like to include them in the study. Photosensitization will present as thickened or “crusty” skin that is more firm that normal.  It occurs commonly in the white skinned areas, ears, nose and rear legs, but can occur anywhere on the body. Involvement in the study will consist of the cost of the campus vet mileage at $1.81/km roundtrip and the cost of the pharmaceuticals needed to treat.
L112: Blood, urine physical examination data, and pictures will be collected from the diseased animal and a healthy individual from the same paddock. Standard therapy will be activated charcoal by mouth and oxytetracycline injectable. The examination, pharmaceutical administration, and veterinary advice will be free.  We are searching for prognostic indicators of intoxicated cattle to better identify cattle that will survive.
L113: Please contact Dr Brandon Fraser (b.fraser@uq.edu.au) for more details.
L114: ## Do you have a cat with diabetes or a diabetic cat in remission?
L115: We are looking for diabetic cats and diabetic cats in remission for three clinical trials that will investigate new treatments and monitoring for this condition. Two studies will investigate the role of a long-acting synthetic drug, exenatide (Bydureon®). The third study will investigate a new generation of glucose monitors that provide immediate glucose values by waving a reader device over a sensor – without needle or sample collection required.
L116: There will be no cost to owners for any diagnostics, study drugs, or monitoring, however, study participants will need to be brought to UQ’s Gatton campus.
L117: Read more 【44†about these trials】.
L118: 
L119: If you would like to participate in this trial, please contact 【45†Dr Aaron M. Herndon】.
